## Company: BDO Unibank, Inc. (BDO)
Sector: Financials / Banks
BDO Unibank Inc. (BDO), originally known as Acme Savings Bank, was acquired by the SM Group in 1976. BDO listed its shares on the Philippine Stock Exchange on May 21, 2002. The Company merged with Equitable PCI Bank in May 2007.

BDO offers an array of products and services including lending (corporate and consumer), deposit-taking, foreign exchange brokering, trust and investments, credit cards, retail cash cards, corporate cash management and remittances. Through its subsidiaries, the Company offers leasing and financing, investment banking, private banking, rural banking, life insurance, property and casualty insurance brokerage, and online and traditional stock brokerage services.

The Company's subsidiaries include BDO Capital & Investment Corporation; BDO Private Bank, Inc.; BDO Leasing and Finance, Inc.; BDO Finance Corporation; and BDO Securities Corporation.

As of December 31, 2024, BDO's network consists of 1,791 operating domestic branches (inclusive of one branch each in Hong Kong and Singapore), 4,923 automated teller machines, 481 universal teller machines, 411 cash accept machines, and 14 overseas remittance and representative offices across Asia, North America, Europe, and the Middle East.

thesis:
BDO Unibank is about as understandable a business as banking gets in the Philippines. It takes deposits, lends money at a spread, and earns fees on insurance, trust, credit cards, and remittances. As the country's largest universal bank by assets — with 1,791 branches strategically embedded inside the SM mall ecosystem — the business model is straightforward and its competitive position in the Philippine consumer economy is hard to dispute. The SM Group relationship is not incidental; it is structural. BDO branches inside SM malls capture captive foot traffic from the Philippines' most visited retail destinations, giving BDO a low-cost acquisition channel for deposits and retail customers that no rival can easily replicate. This is a business any long-term investor can understand and monitor.

The moat is real, though not impenetrable. BDO's scale — 4,923 ATMs, 14 overseas remittance offices, a fully integrated insurance and investment banking subsidiary network — creates meaningful switching costs and brand stickiness. Filipinos rarely switch primary banks, and BDO's penetration of the SM ecosystem gives it a structural deposit-gathering advantage over competitors who must pay more to attract equivalent volume. The network effect compounds over time: more branches attract more deposits, which fund more loans, which generate more fee income. That said, BSP digital banking reforms and the rise of Maya, GCash, and CIMB Bank Philippines represent genuine disruptive pressure on the retail deposit base. BDO is responding through digital investments, but the competitive threat from e-wallets eating at the lower end of its deposit base deserves ongoing scrutiny.

Management quality is credible. Teresita Sy-Coson chairs the board with the Sy family's majority ownership through SM Investments — significant skin in the game with decades of institutional commitment. The ten-year track record bears this out: 11.5% EPS growth, 13.3% net income growth, and 10.9% book value growth compounding over a decade reflect disciplined lending and consistent capital allocation rather than episodic windfalls. The recent half-year result of ₱40.7 billion net income — with Q1 2026 alone at ₱20.1 billion — suggests the growth trajectory remains intact. The return to ASEAN sustainability bond markets and the SME lending partnership with Discovery Capital Finance reflect management actively expanding addressable market rather than resting on incumbency. No red flags emerge from recent disclosures, though the July 2026 "Material Information" disclosure warrants monitoring once details surface publicly.

The valuation is where Rule #1 creates friction. At $126 against a Sticker Price of ₱111 and a MOS buy price of ₱55.54, the stock is technically 127% above the margin of safety entry point. Strict Phil Town methodology says pass here, and that discipline exists for good reason — paying up for quality erodes returns and removes your buffer against being wrong. However, it is worth noting that the Rule #1 calculator applies poorly to banks: the framework uses a P/E multiple anchored to growth rates, but banks globally trade on P/B and ROE, and BDO at 1.1x book with double-digit earnings growth is genuinely cheap by that measure. Analyst consensus targets cluster around ₱168-184, and Alpha Spread's intrinsic value model pegs fair value near ₱215 — implying roughly 33-71% upside from current prices. The P/E of 7.7x and PEG of 0.67x confirm that the market is not pricing in BDO's growth at full value. The 3.4% dividend yield provides income while you wait. Risk factors include a Philippine credit cycle downturn, BSP rate policy shifts compressing net interest margins, and NPL creep if consumer and SME borrowers come under stress.

The bottom line is that BDO is a high-quality business with a durable moat, aligned management, and a consistent growth record — trading at a valuation that is cheap by conventional banking metrics but above the strict Rule #1 MOS threshold. Rule #1 purists should wait for a pullback toward ₱90-100 before initiating a position. Investors comfortable adapting Phil Town's framework to the realities of bank valuation (P/B, ROE) may find the current price an acceptable entry given the quality and trajectory of the business. Watch for the July 2026 material disclosure details, NPL trends in the next quarterly filing, and any regulatory changes from BSP before committing capital.
